anchorData: ANCHOR DEMO (Lesson 1, shown once, never changed). Each beaker holds 10 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl; 50 cm3 of 0.15 mol/dm3 sodium thiosulfate is added. Both solutions are pre-equilibrated in their water baths. Beaker A: 10 C. Beaker B: 50 C. Both are poured at the same moment and placed over identical black crosses. Cross disappears: Beaker B at 35 s, Beaker A at 270 s (4 min 30 s). B is faster by 270 - 35 = 235 s, and 270/35 = 7.7 times. Rate = 1/t: B = 1/35 = 0.0286 s^-1 (28.6 x10^-3 s^-1); A = 1/270 = 0.0037 s^-1 (3.7 x10^-3 s^-1). TEMPERATURE TABLE (Lesson 3; 0.15 mol/dm3 thiosulfate 50 cm3 + 10 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl; class-mean values): 10 C = 270 s, rate 3.7 x10^-3 s^-1; 25 C = 110 s, rate 9.1; 40 C = 52 s, rate 19.2; 55 C = 26 s, rate 38.5. The 10 C row equals Beaker A. The demo 50 C value of 35 s lies between the 40 C (52 s) and 55 C (26 s) rows. CONCENTRATION TABLE (Lesson 4; all at 25 C, 10 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl; thiosulfate volume diluted with water to 50 cm3 total): 0.15 mol/dm3 (50 cm3 thiosulfate + 0 water) = 110 s, rate 9.1 x10^-3 s^-1; 0.12 mol/dm3 (40 + 10) = 138 s, rate 7.2; 0.09 mol/dm3 (30 + 20) = 183 s, rate 5.5; 0.06 mol/dm3 (20 + 30) = 275 s, rate 3.6. Rate / concentration is about 60 for every row, so rate is roughly proportional to concentration. The 0.15 row equals the 25 C row of the temperature table. SURFACE AREA TABLE (Lesson 5; 0.5 g marble chips, CaCO3, in 25 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl at 25 C; CO2 collected in cm3). Large chips (about 10 mm): 30 s = 12, 60 s = 22, 90 s = 31, 120 s = 39. Small chips (about 3 mm): 30 s = 28, 60 s = 50, 90 s = 68, 120 s = 82. Powder: 30 s = 62, 60 s = 100, 90 s = 117, 120 s = 120. Maximum possible CO2 is 0.5 g / 100 g per mol = 0.005 mol, so about 120 cm3 at room temperature; HCl is in excess (0.025 mol). Initial rate over the first 30 s: large 12/30 = 0.40 cm3/s; small 28/30 = 0.93 cm3/s; powder 62/30 = 2.07 cm3/s. Powder is fastest and levels off at 120 cm3. CATALYST DEMO (Lesson 6; 10 cm3 of 3% hydrogen peroxide in a 100 cm3 measuring cylinder with a few drops of detergent; foam height after 30 s): no additive = 0 cm; sand = 0 cm; boiled liver cube (1 cm3) = 0.5 cm; fresh liver cube (1 cm3) = 9 cm. The liver is not used up. Lesson 7 reference values (approximate classroom values): human enzyme amylase works best near 37 C and pH 7; pepsin in the stomach works best near pH 2; uji ferments in about 24 h in a warm kitchen at 30 C but about 48 h at 15 C; fridge temperature is 4 C.
characters: Teacher: Mwalimu Achieng, Grade 10 General Science teacher at a school in Nakuru County; she runs the demos and keeps the Driving Question Board (DQB) on the back wall. Students (use only these named learners): Wanjiru (asks the first 'why' question), Otieno (suggests the particle idea in Lesson 1), Amina (from Mombasa, brings the rusting roof example), Kiprono (from Kericho, brings the tea and uji example). Objects: Beaker A = cold (10 C), Beaker B = warm (50 C); the cold bath represents a cool Nairobi highland morning and the warm bath represents an afternoon in Mombasa or Kisumu. The paper cross is black on white, identical on both sheets. DQB = Driving Question Board; the student notebook is the science notebook. Supporting Kenyan contexts (each only used in the lessons named in the lesson map): mango rotting faster in a hot kiosk (L3), ugali or githeri cooking faster on a hot jiko (L3), antacid tablet fizzing (L4, L5), unga versus whole maize for uji (L5), fresh liver and enzymes in the gut (L6, L7), uji and yoghurt fermentation (L7), rusting of iron roofing sheets in Mombasa (L7), drying and salting fish at Lake Victoria and refrigeration (L7). Institutions: KEMRI for biochemist careers (L8). Fertiliser: Kenya imports and blends fertiliser (for example blending at Athi River); the Haber process is an industrial process used worldwide to make ammonia with an iron catalyst. Do NOT claim that a Haber plant operates at Athi River.
outcome: In the anchor demonstration the cross vanishes at 35 s in warm Beaker B (50 C) and at 270 s in cold Beaker A (10 C), so the warm reaction is 7.7 times faster. The chemicals and amounts were the same; only temperature differed. At higher temperature the particles have more kinetic energy, so they collide more often and with more energy, and a larger fraction of collisions have enough energy to react (effective collisions); the same idea of effective collisions per second then explains concentration, surface area, catalysts and light. Both beakers end with the same amount of sulfur; the factors change the speed of the reaction, not the final amount made.
conventions: Rate of reaction = change in amount of reactant or product per unit time. For the thiosulfate cross method, rate = 1/t, where t is the time in seconds for the cross to disappear; rate is quoted in x10^-3 s^-1 (for example 9.1 x10^-3 s^-1) and is a relative rate, not an absolute one. For the gas method, rate = volume of CO2 (cm3) divided by time (s), in cm3/s. Always say 'rate' for speed of reaction and never 'rate of heat'. Temperature in C; concentration in mol/dm3; volume in cm3; mass in g; time in s. The cross is 'gone' when the observer looking down from above can no longer see any part of the black lines (same observer, same bench lighting, same beaker type if possible). Reaction: sodium thiosulfate + hydrochloric acid -> sodium chloride + sulfur + sulfur dioxide + water; Na2S2O3(aq) + 2HCl(aq) -> 2NaCl(aq) + S(s) + SO2(g) + H2O(l). The yellow precipitate is sulfur. Reaction: CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g). Reaction: 2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2 (catalysed by catalase in liver). Safety: SO2 is an irritant, so use small quantities, ventilated room, rinse the beakers straight after the cross vanishes, and wear goggles. Variables: independent variable = the factor you change; dependent variable = time (or rate); control variables = everything else kept constant. Use 'collision theory' and the terms 'particles', 'effective collisions', 'activation energy' (minimum energy needed for a collision to react). Do not use 'frequency of collisions' to mean energy. A catalyst speeds up a reaction, provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy and is not used up; an enzyme is a biological catalyst. Light is a source of energy for some reactions (photosynthesis, silver bromide in photographic film) and is not a catalyst. Graphs: plot the independent variable on the x-axis and the rate on the y-axis; for gas data plot volume on the y-axis against time. Gradient (slope) of a volume-time curve = rate. Use the data in anchorData exactly; do not invent other numbers for these experiments. Do not call the demo a 'race'. Each lesson uses the 5 phases: Predict, Observe, Explain, DQB, Model Building.

lessonMap.focus: What Is a Rate of Reaction? Launching the Disappearing Cross
lessonMap.teaches: Rate of reaction is how fast reactants are used up or products formed, and it can be measured in three ways: time for a change (precipitate), volume of gas, or loss of mass.
lessonMap.buildsOn: None; this is the launch. Uses students' everyday ideas about fast and slow changes (mango rotting, ugali cooking).
lessonMap.usesData: The anchor demo only: Beaker A 10 C, 270 s; Beaker B 50 C, 35 s; 7.7 times faster. No tables beyond this.

lessonMap.focus: Measuring Reaction Rates: Designing a Fair Test
lessonMap.teaches: How to turn a time measurement into a rate (rate = 1/t) and how to plan a fair test by naming the independent, dependent and control variables.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 1: the demo, the definition of rate, and the DQB questions about why B was faster.
lessonMap.usesData: Demo times 35 s and 270 s converted to rates 28.6 and 3.7 x10^-3 s^-1; the thiosulfate-HCl quantities (50 cm3 and 10 cm3) as the controls; no new results.

lessonMap.teaches: Higher temperature increases the rate because particles have more kinetic energy, collide more often and more energetically, so more collisions are effective (first statement of collision theory).
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 1 (the demo to be explained) and Lesson 2 (rate = 1/t, fair-test design, data table).
lessonMap.usesData: The temperature table: 10 C 270 s, 25 C 110 s, 40 C 52 s, 55 C 26 s and their rates 3.7, 9.1, 19.2, 38.5 x10^-3 s^-1; link back to demo 50 C = 35 s.

lessonMap.teaches: Higher concentration means more particles per unit volume, so collisions are more frequent, and rate is roughly proportional to concentration.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 3 (collision theory, the 25 C result of 110 s) and Lesson 2 (variables, graph plotting of rate).
lessonMap.usesData: The concentration table: 0.15, 0.12, 0.09, 0.06 mol/dm3 with times 110, 138, 183, 275 s and rates 9.1, 7.2, 5.5, 3.6 x10^-3 s^-1.

lessonMap.teaches: Breaking a solid into smaller pieces exposes more surface for collisions, so the rate rises; rate from a gas-volume curve is read as its gradient.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 3 and 4 (collision theory, more effective collisions per second) and Lesson 1 (gas volume as a way to measure rate).
lessonMap.usesData: The surface area table: large, small and powder CO2 volumes at 30, 60, 90, 120 s; initial rates 0.40, 0.93, 2.07 cm3/s; maximum 120 cm3.

lessonMap.teaches: A catalyst (such as the enzyme catalase) speeds up a reaction through an alternative pathway with lower activation energy without being used up; light supplies energy for some reactions.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 3 to 5 (frequency and energy of collisions as the only factors so far; students now see a rate change without a change of temperature, concentration or size).
lessonMap.usesData: The catalyst demo: foam height 0, 0, 0.5 and 9 cm for no additive, sand, boiled liver and fresh liver; the Haber process and photosynthesis as discussion; no new numbers.

lessonMap.focus: Applying the Model to Biological, Chemical and Physical Processes in Kenya
lessonMap.teaches: Several factors act together in real systems, and optimum conditions exist: enzymes work best at a certain temperature and pH, whereas preservation slows reactions by cooling, drying and salting.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 3 to 6 (all four factors and collision theory); Lesson 1 DQB questions are reviewed for answers.
lessonMap.usesData: Lesson 7 reference values: amylase near 37 C and pH 7, pepsin near pH 2, uji 24 h at 30 C versus 48 h at 15 C, fridge 4 C; revisit the temperature table (L3) as the evidence for cooling food.

lessonMap.focus: Model Building, Assessment and Community Connection
lessonMap.teaches: Putting the final model to use: predicting and explaining an unfamiliar Kenyan scenario with the collision-theory model and choosing which factor to change to solve a real problem.
lessonMap.buildsOn: All of lessons 1 to 7: the cumulative model, the DQB, the four factors and the application contexts.
lessonMap.usesData: Return to the anchor demo (35 s versus 270 s, 7.7 times faster) for the final explanation; cite one row from the temperature, concentration or surface area tables as evidence; a new scenario uses no new numbers from anchorData.
